chunks.heading: How do I play Hype Check?
chunks.text: You get ten claims about quantum computers, one at a time. Tap one of three buttons: Real today, Maybe someday, or Hype or myth. The game then shows the right bin with a short reason, and you tap Next card. A round always has 3 real, 3 maybe-someday and 4 hype claims. You pass with 7 or more right, and 9 or more earns three stars. New cards deals a different set. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: How do I decide which bin a claim belongs in?
chunks.text: Ask two questions. Can this be done or seen today? Then it is Real today. If not, is it a sensible goal that researchers are working towards but that needs bigger or less noisy machines? Then it is Maybe someday. If the claim misunderstands how quantum computers work, or promises something they will not do, it is Hype or myth. Many claims have a true core, so read the reason after each card.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck. How do I get better at Hype Check?
chunks.text: Keep three ideas in mind. Quantum computers are specialist machines for a few kinds of problems, not faster versions of everything. Today's machines are small and noisy. And the speed-ups come from interference, which cancels wrong answers, not from trying every answer at once. When a claim sounds exciting, look for the word that makes it too big, such as everything, replace, or instantly.

chunks.heading: Why is a claim Maybe someday when scientists say it is possible?
chunks.text: Possible in principle is not the same as real today. Maybe someday means the idea is sound, but the machines are not big or reliable enough yet, or the research is still open. Real today means you can do it or see it now. The reason shown after each card says which of the two it is.

chunks.heading: Why did I get a card wrong when it sounded true?
chunks.text: Many myths contain a true part. The wording matters: a quantum computer being faster at some problems is true, faster at everything is a myth. Read the reason on the card to see exactly where the claim goes too far, then look for the same pattern in the next card.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Hype Check show?
chunks.text: Passing means you can tell the real picture from the hype: quantum computers are real, promising and limited. Passing a round counts as completing the game in the course. The three bins simplify a messy picture, so real experts often say it depends. The reason on each card is the real lesson, even when you got the card right.

chunks.heading: How do I play Quantum Heist?
chunks.text: There are three stages and three shields (hearts). In each stage you set up your agent's quantum state, then tap the breach button. A wrong state trips the alarm and costs a shield, and losing all three ends the run. Stage 1 has two doors, Stage 2 has a wave trap, and Stage 3 has a 3D Bloch sphere radar that you steer with the arrow pad. Pressing the H, X and Z keys is free; only the breach button can set off the alarm. Rules explains the controls and Hint shows the next move. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: What do the H, X and Z keys do in Quantum Heist?
chunks.text: H (Hadamard) spreads a definite door evenly over both doors, and gathers an even spread back to one door. X swaps the two doors, so Door 0 becomes Door 1. Z leaves the chance at each door alone but flips the sign (the phase) of the Door 1 part. You cannot see a sign in the door percentages, yet it changes what the next H does.

chunks.heading: Why does the scanner not catch me when I am split 50/50?
chunks.text: The camera fires if you are 100% at one door. A 50/50 split leaves it with nothing to aim at, which is a playful picture of superposition: before any measurement the agent has no single door. This is a simplified model, because a real measurement would still find the qubit at one door, with 50% chance for each.

chunks.heading: Why does Stage 2 care about a sign when the percentages look the same?
chunks.text: Two different states can both show 50/50 at the doors. They differ in the sign between the two parts, which is the phase. Waves from the two parts can add up or cancel out, like ripples on water, depending on that sign. The trap's wave cancels only for one of the two signs.

chunks.heading: How does the Bloch sphere radar in Stage 3 work?
chunks.text: Every single-qubit state is a point on the Bloch sphere. The north pole is |0>, the south pole is |1>, and the equator holds the 50/50 states. How far around the equator you are is the phase. The arrow pad tilts the crosshair up and down, which changes the chances, or turns it left and right, which changes the phase. You are ready when the crosshair is close to the target ring.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Quantum Heist. What can I try?
chunks.text: Read the mission objective, then look at your door percentages and ask what is different between where you are and what is asked. Is it the chance at the doors, the sign, or the place on the sphere? Try each key once and watch what changes. After an alarm, Retry infiltration puts you back at the start of the stage. The Hint button shows the next move whenever you want it.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Quantum Heist show?
chunks.text: You have met superposition, phase and the Bloch sphere in one story. Honesty note: this is a simplified model. Real state preparation uses gates, and a real measurement gives only one outcome.

chunks.heading: How do I play the Quantum Penny Paradox?
chunks.text: A penny starts on Heads, which is |0>. Each round has three steps: Dr. Quantum plays a move, you play a move, then Dr. Quantum plays again and the coin is measured. Dr. Quantum wins on Heads and you win on Tails. You start in classical mode, where your moves are FLIP (X) and KEEP (I). The Unlock button switches to quantum mode, which adds a third move, the phase flip (Z). Play as many rounds as you like; there is no timer. It is David Meyer's 1999 game.

chunks.heading: Why does Dr. Quantum always win in classical mode?
chunks.text: Dr. Quantum's first move, H, puts the coin into an equal superposition, |+>. Flipping swaps the two equal halves, which gives exactly the same state back, so a flip does nothing. Keeping does nothing too. Dr. Quantum's second H then undoes the first one, and the coin lands on Heads every time.

chunks.heading: What does the quantum move do?
chunks.text: The phase flip (Z) changes the sign between the two halves, so |+> becomes |->. That is a different state even though it still looks 50/50, and no classical move can reach it. Dr. Quantum's second H turns |-> into |1>, so the coin lands on Tails every time.

chunks.heading: Why does a phase flip beat Dr. Quantum when the coin looks the same?
chunks.text: The chances of Heads and Tails are not the whole state. The sign between the two halves is part of the state too, and H turns a plus into Heads and a minus into Tails. This is interference at work: the two halves add up for one outcome and cancel for the other.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck. Can I ever beat Dr. Quantum?
chunks.text: Not in classical mode, because flip and keep lead to the same result. Switch on quantum mode with the Unlock button and look at the extra move you are given. Think about what that move changes that a flip does not: a flip changes which half is which, but a flip cannot change the sign between them.

chunks.heading: Would the Hadamard gate also beat Dr. Quantum?
chunks.text: No. If you played H as your move, the coin would go from |+> to |0>, and Dr. Quantum's second H would take it back to |+>, so the final measurement would be a 50/50 coin flip. Only a move that changes the sign, such as Z, forces Tails.

chunks.heading: Is the Quantum Penny Paradox a real quantum game?
chunks.text: Yes. David Meyer described it in 1999 as one of the first quantum games. The app runs the ideal version, with perfect gates and no noise. Dr. Quantum is not cheating: a quantum player simply has moves that a classical player does not.

chunks.heading: What does finishing the Quantum Penny Paradox show?
chunks.text: Winning shows that the chances of Heads and Tails are not the whole state: the sign between the two halves matters too, and interference turns that sign into a different outcome. A move that no classical player has is enough to turn a lost game into a won one. The game is accurate, though it is the ideal noiseless version of Meyer's game.

chunks.heading: How do I play Schrödinger's Stealth?
chunks.text: There are three sectors, each a corridor of laser checkpoints. Every checkpoint is a slot shaped like a quantum state: vertical for |0>, horizontal for |1>, 45 degrees for |+>, and the opposite diagonal for |->. Your agent starts vertical. Use the gadgets [H] TILT, [X] FLIP and [Z] PHASE to change your stance until it matches the slot, then slip through. A match passes with certainty. If it does not match, the laser measures you: you slip through with exactly the chance shown (a 50% match passes half the time), and otherwise your state collapses and the alarm goes up by 25 to 40 percent. At 100 percent the run is over. Using gadgets is free. A gadget pulses when it is the one that helps.

chunks.heading: What are the blue and pink scanners?
chunks.text: A scanner is a measurement in a chosen basis. The blue scanner asks whether you are |0> or |1>. The pink scanner asks whether you are |+> or |->, and the purple scanner is the pink one set for the negative diagonal. If your state matches what a scanner is asking about, the answer is certain and nothing is disturbed. If it does not match, the answer is random with chances given by the Born rule, and the measurement collapses your state into whichever answer came out.

chunks.heading: What does the percent chance of stealth mean?
chunks.text: It is the chance that this scanner finds you in exactly the state its slot is shaped for. When your state is close enough to a match (above 95%) the game shows 100% STEALTH and you pass for certain. Anything lower is a gamble: the laser measures you, you slip through with exactly that chance, and otherwise you are caught.

chunks.heading: Why does the same H gadget sometimes take me to diagonal and sometimes back to vertical?
chunks.text: H swaps the two views of the qubit. From vertical |0> it gives the diagonal |+>, and from the diagonal |+> it gives vertical |0> again. Applying H twice does nothing at all. So the same gadget goes both ways, depending on where you are.

chunks.heading: What does the Z phase gadget do when my shape does not seem to change?
chunks.text: Z flips the sign of the |1> part. For vertical |0> and horizontal |1> that makes no visible difference, because the sign is only a global factor. For a diagonal it matters a lot: |+> becomes |->, the other diagonal. So Z is only useful once you are in a superposition.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Schrödinger's Stealth. What should I do?
chunks.text: Compare two things: the shape of the slot at the checkpoint and the shape of your agent. Then ask which single gadget turns your shape into theirs. The gadget that helps pulses. You can try gadgets as often as you like, because only stepping through the slot can raise the alarm.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Schrödinger's Stealth show?
chunks.text: Measurement depends on the question being asked. A state that matches the question gets a certain answer and is left alone, and a state that does not match gets a random answer and is changed. That is why measuring in the wrong basis disturbs a qubit.

chunks.heading: How do I play Bloch Runner?
chunks.text: Your qubit is the red arrow on the Bloch sphere, and the ghost marker is the target. Each level gives you a few gate buttons. Tap a gate to apply it and the arrow moves. Reach the ghost to clear the checkpoint. Undo removes your last move, Restart clears them all, and Hint gives a clue. You also have a move limit, which is the shortest solution plus three. Stars: par or fewer moves earns 3, one over par earns 2, more earns 1. Show the math lists the amplitudes and the Bloch coordinates. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: What does each gate do on the Bloch sphere?
chunks.text: Every gate is a rotation of the sphere. X, Y and Z are half-turns about their own axes. S is a quarter-turn and T an eighth-turn about the vertical Z axis, and S-dagger is the quarter-turn the other way. H tips the pole onto the equator and back; it is a half-turn about the axis between X and Z. Gates that turn about the vertical axis change the direction you face around the equator but not your height.

chunks.heading: Why does a gate sometimes seem to do nothing to the arrow?
chunks.text: A rotation about an axis leaves a point on that axis where it is. At the north pole, spinning about the vertical axis does not move the arrow, so Z, S and T leave |0> alone. Only the overall phase changes, and nobody can measure that. The same thing happens at the south pole.

chunks.heading: What do the |0> and |1> percentage bars mean?
chunks.text: They are the chances of getting 0 or 1 if you measured the qubit now. At the north pole it is 100% for 0, on the equator it is 50% each, and at the south pole it is 100% for 1. The bars do not show the direction around the equator, which is the phase. Two points on the equator share the same bars but are different states, which is why you sometimes need the sphere and not the bars.

chunks.heading: What does par mean, and why can I run out of moves?
chunks.text: Par is the fewest moves that solve the level, found by a search. Your move limit is par plus three, so you can wander a little but not forever. If you run out, Undo a step or Restart and try another route. Running out of moves costs nothing; it only means you have not found a short enough path yet.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Bloch Runner. How do I plan a path?
chunks.text: Look at the arrow and the ghost, and ask two things. Does the ghost sit at a different height, meaning a different chance of 0 or 1? Or is it at the same height but facing a different direction around the sphere? Gates like X and H usually change height, and gates like Z, S and T turn you around the vertical axis. Tap Hint if you want a clue.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Bloch Runner show?
chunks.text: Every single-qubit gate is a rotation, and you can steer a qubit to any place on the sphere by combining a few of them. The Bloch sphere is an exact picture for one qubit, so this game is accurate. It only has one qubit, so entanglement is not part of it.

chunks.heading: How do I play the Photon Escape Room?
chunks.text: A photon enters from the source on the left and leaves through the top or bottom door on the right. Between them are slots. Tap a slot to cycle what is in it: empty, a beam splitter, or in some rooms a phase shifter with settings of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees on the lower path. The goal list turns green as you meet each goal. Fire a photon sends one photon and shows which door clicks. The percentages on the doors are chances, and the beam brightness shows the chance on each path. Some rooms need a minimum number of beam splitters. Reset and Hint are available, and there is no timer.

chunks.heading: What do the beam splitter and the phase shifter do?
chunks.text: A beam splitter sends a photon down both paths at once, in superposition. A phase shifter delays the lower path by part of a wavelength. A second beam splitter then brings the two paths back together, and the photon's two possibilities add or cancel at each door depending on the phase between them. That adding and cancelling is interference.

chunks.heading: Why do two beam splitters not just give 25% for each door?
chunks.text: Probabilities only multiply when the paths cannot interfere. Here the two paths come back together at the second splitter, so their amplitudes combine and can add or cancel. The result can be 100% at one door and 0% at the other. Change the phase and the numbers change smoothly, so you can watch them.

chunks.heading: Why does the photon click only one door when the percentages are not 100%?
chunks.text: One photon is always found at just one door. The percentages are the chances, and you only see them in the clicks after firing many photons. The tally under the button counts your clicks so far. Your goals are about the chances, not about any single click.

chunks.heading: Why can a saboteur make the dark door click?
chunks.text: A blocker in one path removes the interference, because only one path is left to reach the last splitter. With a single path the photon is sent 50/50, so a door that was dark with both paths can now click. That is the idea behind the bomb test: a change in where clicks can happen reveals that something is in the path.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in the Photon Escape Room. What can I try?
chunks.text: Change one slot at a time and watch the door percentages and the goal list. Ask whether you need a splitter in a slot at all, and what the phase does to the numbers. The percentages move smoothly, so you can tell which way to go. If a room needs a minimum number of splitters, do all of them. Tap Hint for a clue.

chunks.heading: What does finishing the Photon Escape Room show?
chunks.text: A single photon takes both paths at once, and where the paths agree the photon can exit and where they cancel the door stays dark. Interference is the tool quantum algorithms use to boost right answers. The model is the real single-photon maths, so the game is accurate.

chunks.heading: How do I play Alice and Bob?
chunks.text: A guard asks Alice and Bob a question each, 0 or 1, and each answers 0 or 1 without talking. The door opens when their answers differ only if both were asked 1; otherwise their answers must match. Part 1: tap the buttons to set what each person says for each question and watch the table show which of the four question pairs you win. Run 100 rounds plays random questions. After flipping at least four answers you can go to Part 2, where the pair share an entangled state. There you set four measurement angles in 22.5 degree steps. You need an 80 percent win chance to open the door.

chunks.heading: Why can I never win all four question pairs with a classical plan?
chunks.text: Three of the four question pairs ask for matching answers, and one asks for different answers. If you follow the three matching rules, every answer ends up equal to every other, which breaks the fourth rule. The game checked all 16 possible plans: the best classical score is 3 of 4, which is 75 percent.

chunks.heading: What are the angles in Part 2?
chunks.text: Each angle is the direction in which that person measures their half of the entangled pair, chosen according to the question they were asked. The win chance for each question pair depends on how far apart Alice's angle and Bob's angle are. The table shows the chance for each question pair, and the total is their average.

chunks.heading: Why does Run 100 rounds not give exactly the win chance?
chunks.text: The rounds are random: random questions, and random measurement outcomes with the stated chances. A hundred rounds wobble around the true chance, a bit like a hundred coin flips giving not exactly fifty heads. More rounds would settle closer to the exact number.

chunks.heading: Does this mean Alice and Bob are sending messages faster than light?
chunks.text: No. Each person's own answers look completely random. The pattern only appears when the two lists are compared afterwards, using a normal message. Entanglement gives correlations that no shared classical plan can match, but it cannot be used to send a signal.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Part 2 of Alice and Bob. What can I try?
chunks.text: Change one angle at a time and watch the table and the total. The win chance for a question pair depends on the gap between the two angles used for it. Three of the question pairs want the gap small and one wants it large, so look for angles that balance the two needs. The game shows its own hint if you stay under the target.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Alice and Bob show?
chunks.text: No team using only a shared plan can beat 75 percent, and an entangled pair lets them reach about 85 percent, the best the maths allows. That is a Bell test (the CHSH game). The game is a simplified model: it uses an ideal entangled pair and lets you pick the measurement angles directly, with no noise.

chunks.heading: How do I play Teleport Relay?
chunks.text: A qubit message travels along a chain: Alice, one or more repeaters, then Bob. At each hop a fresh Bell pair links the sender and the receiver. The sender measures, and the game shows the two bits they get. The receiver's qubit is now a twisted copy of the message, and you add fix gates (up to three, in order) and tap Send it on. If the red arrow lands on the ghost marker, the hop is complete. Wrong tries cost stars and there is no timer. Rule shows the answer table, which is a spoiler, and Hint gives a clue.

chunks.heading: What does the ghost marker mean, and what is the red arrow?
chunks.text: The ghost marker is the original message. The red arrow is the qubit that the receiving repeater really has right now. A hop is correct when the arrow sits exactly on the ghost, and the message then moves on to the next repeater. The percent in a wrong try says how close the two are: 100 is perfect, and 50 is no better than a coin flip.

chunks.heading: Why does the receiver need the two bits to fix the qubit?
chunks.text: The measurement can leave the receiver's qubit damaged in four possible ways: not at all, with a bit flip, with a phase flip, or with both. Without the two bits the receiver cannot tell which one happened, and their qubit looks random. The bits travel by an ordinary route, so teleportation cannot send anything faster than light.

chunks.heading: Where does the original qubit go, and can I keep a copy?
chunks.text: The sender's measurement destroys the original, so teleportation moves a qubit and does not copy it. Copying an unknown quantum state is impossible, which is the no-cloning theorem. Each hop also uses up one Bell pair.

chunks.heading: Why do some levels list gates I do not need?
chunks.text: Some panels include extra gates to tempt you. Think about what kinds of damage the measurement can cause: a bit flip, a phase flip, both, or neither. Gates that cannot undo any of those are decoys. One hop may even need no gate at all.

chunks.heading: Does the order of the fix gates matter?
chunks.text: When two fixes are needed, X then Z and Z then X differ only by an overall sign, and nobody can measure that. So either order works. For the game, what matters is which fixes you include.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Teleport Relay. What should I do?
chunks.text: Look at the two bits: each of them is connected to one kind of damage. Ask what each bit being 0 or 1 means, and try the level's Hint. You can also try a fix and send it: a wrong try costs a star but shows you how close you were. If you want to see the whole table, Rule shows it, but it is a spoiler.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Teleport Relay show?
chunks.text: Each hop used one Bell pair and two ordinary bits, and the qubit itself never travelled. Chains of hops like this are the idea behind a quantum network. The game follows the real protocol with fixed bits so every level plays the same way each time.

chunks.heading: How do I play Gate Deck?
chunks.text: Each level names a target gate that you must build. Your hand has cards: gates on a particular qubit, and CNOT cards written control to target. Tap a card to play it. Cards run left to right and each card can be used once, and you do not have to use all of them. The circuit preview shows one row per qubit, with a dot for the control and a plus-in-a-circle for the target. Below it, test inputs show a green check for every input where your circuit acts like the target. When all are green, you have built the gate. Undo, Clear and Hint are there to help, and stars reward the shortest recipe. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: What does matching the target on each test input mean?
chunks.text: A gate is defined by what it does to every input. The test inputs are each basis state plus some equal mixtures of basis states. If your circuit gives the same result as the target on all of them, it is the same gate. A red cross tells you which input still behaves differently, which is a clue about what is missing.

chunks.heading: What does up to a global phase mean?
chunks.text: Multiplying a whole state by a constant like -1 or i changes nothing you can measure. So two circuits that differ only by such a factor count as the same gate, and for some gates two different card orders are both accepted.

chunks.heading: How do I read a CNOT card?
chunks.text: A card such as CNOT 0 to 1 means qubit 0 is the control and qubit 1 is the target. The target is flipped only when the control is 1. In the preview, q0 is the top row. A CNOT in the opposite direction is a different card, and sandwiching a CNOT with Hadamards on both qubits changes which one acts as the control.

chunks.heading: Why does wrapping a gate in Hadamards change what it does?
chunks.text: H changes the point of view: it swaps the Z-axis view of the qubit with the X-axis view. A gate applied in the new view looks different from the old one. For example, a bit flip seen through H becomes a phase flip, and the other way round. The sandwich H, gate, H is how many gates are built from others.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Gate Deck. How do I find the recipe?
chunks.text: Play a card and look at which test inputs turn green or stay red. Ask what your cards do on their own and what the target does, and which input is still wrong. The order of the cards matters, so try rearranging with Undo. The Hint gives the idea for the level. Cards you do not need are decoys.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Gate Deck show?
chunks.text: Real quantum hardware offers only a few native gates, and everything else is a recipe built from them. You built Z, X, S, Y, a reversed CNOT, a SWAP and a CZ from other gates. The game is accurate: it checks your circuit against the target with the real maths.

chunks.heading: How do I play Oracle Detective?
chunks.text: A hidden function is either constant, with every locker showing the same light, or balanced, with exactly half on and half off. Tap a locker to open it and see its light. Each opened locker counts as one question. In later cases a quantum informant can be asked once, and that also counts as one question. When you are ready, press Constant or Balanced. Stars: a wrong verdict earns none, a lucky guess one, a proven verdict with more than two questions two, and a proven verdict with two or fewer three. New file replays the case with a different function. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: What counts as proof that a function is balanced or constant?
chunks.text: Two lockers that disagree prove the function is balanced, because a constant function never disagrees. To prove it constant you must open more than half of the lockers and find them all the same, because a balanced function has exactly half of each value. The panel What you can prove so far tells you where you stand.

chunks.heading: Why can I not be sure after a few lockers all agree?
chunks.text: A balanced function could still show the same value in its first few lockers by luck. Only when you have opened more than half of them is it impossible for a balanced function to show all the same. Until then, agreement is a hint and not a proof.

chunks.heading: How does the quantum informant answer with only one question?
chunks.text: She puts all the locker numbers into superposition, asks the oracle once, and applies Hadamards again. Each locker's answer becomes a plus or minus sign, and the signs interfere. If every locker is the same, everything lands on the all-zeros reading. If half are on, the signs cancel exactly and all zeros never comes up. This is the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm.

chunks.heading: What does the readout from the informant mean?
chunks.text: It is the result of measuring the input qubits, written as a string of 0s and 1s. All zeros means the function is constant. Anything else means it is balanced. In the game the informant is always right, because the simulation has no noise.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Oracle Detective. What should I do?
chunks.text: Look at What you can prove so far and ask what evidence would settle the question. Each locker and each informant question costs one question, and fewer questions earn more stars. If the informant is out of town, you have to use lockers. If she is in town, think about which is cheaper. The Hint reminds you what each question costs.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Oracle Detective show?
chunks.text: Classically you may have to open more than half of the lockers to be sure, and the quantum informant needed one question. It is a small, honest example of interference beating brute force, though nobody needs this exact problem solved. The game is accurate because the informant runs the real Deutsch-Jozsa circuit.

chunks.heading: How do I play Qubit Surgeon?
chunks.text: Each patient is one qubit spread over three data qubits, Q1, Q2 and Q3. Noise may have flipped some of them. A probe compares two qubits and tells you whether they agree or differ, and it never reads their values. Use probes, decide which qubit to flip back, and tap Flip Q1, Flip Q2, Flip Q3, or Leave alone. A ward is a set of patients, and stars reward the method: three stars need every fix proven by probes with no spare probes, two need no wrong fixes, and one allows a single wrong fix. Patients nobody could save do not count against you. There is no timer.

chunks.heading: Why can I not just look at the qubits?
chunks.text: Reading a data qubit measures it, which forces it to be a plain 0 or 1 and destroys the superposition that carried the encoded information. That is why probes only compare qubits. The Look directly button shows what happens: the patient is lost.

chunks.heading: What does a probe tell me?
chunks.text: A probe compares two qubits and says whether they agree or differ, without saying what either one is. A flipped qubit disagrees with its neighbours, so different probes point at different qubits. Think about which pattern of agree and differ each single flipped qubit would produce.

chunks.heading: Why are two probes enough?
chunks.text: Two different probes already give four possible patterns, which is enough to tell apart no flip, and a flip of each of the three qubits. The third probe on the tray is just the other two combined, so it adds nothing. Extra probes only cost time and stars.

chunks.heading: Why should I leave a healthy patient alone?
chunks.text: If every comparison agrees, no single qubit flipped. Flipping a qubit anyway would create an error in a healthy patient. Leave alone is a real option and sometimes the right answer.

chunks.heading: Why can two flips at once fool the code?
chunks.text: The code works like a vote: it assumes the one odd qubit out is the flipped one. When two qubits flip, the odd one out is actually the healthy one, so the fix flips the wrong qubit and the whole encoded qubit ends up flipped. The code can undo one flip, not two. That is why protection is not perfect: the chance of losing the qubit falls from p to about 3p squared minus 2p cubed.

chunks.heading: I'm stuck in Qubit Surgeon. What should I try?
chunks.text: Use a probe and read the answer, then use a second, different probe. Look at the panel What you can prove so far, which tells you when the evidence is enough. Ask what each flipped qubit would have done to the probes. The Hint explains the pattern if you want it.

chunks.heading: What does finishing Qubit Surgeon show?
chunks.text: Errors can be found without ever reading the data, just by comparing qubits. Real machines use bigger codes that also catch phase flips, and they need many physical qubits for one reliable logical qubit. This game is a simplified model: it protects only against bit flips and keeps the noise to a few simple cases. The Noise Lab shows how the failure rate falls over thousands of runs.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Single-Qubit Lab?
chunks.text: The red arrow on the Bloch sphere is your qubit. Move it with the two sliders (latitude and longitude), the preset state buttons (|0>, |1>, |+>, |->, |+i>, |-i>) or the gates H, X, Z and S. The readout shows the chances of measuring 0 and 1. Sample 100 Shots measures the same state a hundred times. Try Guided Experiments walks you through superposition, phase and the bit flip, and the Match Target State Challenge asks you to steer the arrow onto a target. Show the math lists the exact amplitudes.

chunks.heading: What do latitude and longitude mean?
chunks.text: Latitude (theta) is the angle down from the north pole: 0 degrees is |0>, 90 degrees is the equator and 180 degrees is |1>. It sets the chances: the chance of 1 is sin squared of theta over two. Longitude (phi) is how far around the sphere you are, which is the relative phase between the two parts. It does not change the chances of 0 and 1 at all, but it changes what later gates do.

chunks.heading: Why do |+> and |-> show the same percentages?
chunks.text: Both sit on the equator, so a measurement gives 0 or 1 with 50% each. They differ only in phase, which is invisible to that measurement. A Hadamard gate turns the phase difference into a difference you can see: H takes |+> to |0> and |-> to |1>. That is why phase matters even though you cannot read it directly.

chunks.heading: Why do 100 shots not give exactly the predicted split?
chunks.text: The chances describe what happens over many runs. Each single measurement is random, so a hundred of them wobble around the prediction, like a hundred coin flips not giving exactly fifty heads. More shots settle closer to the prediction. The Shots + Histogram Lab shows this in detail.

chunks.heading: What do the H, X, Z and S gates do to the arrow?
chunks.text: Every gate rotates the sphere. X is a half-turn about the X axis, which swaps the poles. Z is a half-turn about the vertical axis, which swings the arrow to the opposite side of the equator and leaves the poles alone. S is a quarter-turn about the vertical axis. H tips a pole onto the equator and back, a half-turn about the axis between X and Z.

chunks.heading: How do I match the target in the challenge?
chunks.text: Look at the ghost target and ask whether it is higher or lower than the arrow (latitude), or in a different direction around the sphere (longitude). The preset buttons snap to the common states, and the gates move you in whole steps. You are done when the arrow is close enough to the target, not exactly on it.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Single-Qubit Lab?
chunks.text: Three things. A qubit's state is a point on a sphere, not just a 0 or a 1. The chances of 0 and 1 depend only on the height of the arrow, and the direction around the sphere (phase) is hidden until a gate turns it into a chance. And a measurement always gives a plain 0 or 1, never a blend. This lab is exact for one qubit and has no noise.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Shots + Histogram Lab?
chunks.text: Choose a state: one tilted qubit, a Bell pair, or three qubits that each had an H. For the tilted qubit, the slider sets its tilt. Choose how many shots per run (10, 100, 1,000 or 10,000) and tap Run: that many measurements are added to the histogram. The bars are what was measured, and the dashed marker on each bar is what the maths predicts. The clear button empties the tally.

chunks.heading: Why is the histogram never exactly the prediction?
chunks.text: Each shot is one random draw from the probabilities, so a finite number of shots wobbles around them. The typical size of the wobble is the square root of p times (1 minus p) divided by the number of shots, so ten times the shots shrinks it only about threefold. A real quantum computer returns one bitstring per run, so every result on hardware is a histogram like this.

chunks.heading: How many shots do I need?
chunks.text: It depends on how precisely you want to know a probability. To halve the wobble you need four times the shots. Pinning a 50/50 outcome down to about one percent takes thousands of shots. The banner under the chart tells you the typical wobble for the number of shots you have run so far.

chunks.heading: Why does the Bell pair only show 00 and 11?
chunks.text: The two qubits are entangled so that their answers always agree. The outcomes 01 and 10 have chance zero, and 00 and 11 each have 50%. Each qubit alone is a fair coin flip, but together they never disagree. Bitstrings read from the highest qubit on the left down to qubit 0 on the right.

chunks.heading: Why does three qubits with H give eight outcomes of 12.5% each?
chunks.text: Each H puts one qubit into an even superposition, and with three qubits there are eight possible bitstrings, all with the same amplitude. Each has a chance of one in eight, which is 12.5%. It is the same idea as flipping three fair coins and listing the eight possible results.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Shots + Histogram Lab?
chunks.text: A single measurement tells you almost nothing about a quantum state: you only see the odds by repeating it. As the shots grow, the bars settle onto the dashed predictions, slowly, because the wobble shrinks only with the square root of the shots. The lab samples the exact probabilities, so it is accurate but has no hardware noise.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Circuit Lab?
chunks.text: Choose 1, 2 or 3 qubits; every wire starts at 0 and time runs left to right. Pick a gate (H, X, Y, Z, S, T) and tap a cell in the grid to place it. For a CNOT, pick CNOT, tap the control cell, then tap the target cell in the same column. Erase removes a gate and the bin clears the circuit. Run 1000 shots samples the circuit, and the famous circuits (such as a Bell pair) fill in the grid for you. The bars show the exact probability of each result, and Show the math lists the amplitudes.

chunks.heading: How do I read the bitstrings in the Circuit Lab?
chunks.text: Bitstrings read from the highest qubit on the left down to qubit 0 on the right, the same order as Qiskit. So with three qubits, 100 means q2 is 1 and q1 and q0 are 0. This is the opposite of the order the wires are drawn, which has q0 at the top.

chunks.heading: Why do Z, S and T seem to do nothing in the Circuit Lab?
chunks.text: They only change the phase of the 1 part, which does not change the chance of 0 or 1 by itself. Their effect shows up when a later gate, usually an H, turns the phase difference into a difference in probabilities. Put an H before and after a Z and watch the result change.

chunks.heading: How does a CNOT create entanglement?
chunks.text: A CNOT flips the target qubit only when the control is 1. If the control is in superposition, the target is flipped in one branch and not in the other, so the two qubits can no longer be described separately. An H on one qubit followed by a CNOT from that qubit to the other makes a Bell pair, whose results always agree.

chunks.heading: Why does the measured result differ a little from the prediction?
chunks.text: The bars show the exact probabilities, and the measured result is 1,000 random shots from them. A thousand shots wobble by a few percent around the exact value, which is normal. The exact bars are what an ideal quantum computer would do, and a real one adds noise on top.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Circuit Lab?
chunks.text: A circuit is a recipe: gates in order, then a measurement. Hadamards create superpositions and interference decides which results are likely, which is why a gate that seems to do nothing can still matter later. A CNOT is how qubits become entangled. This is an exact simulator for up to 3 qubits, so it shows what an ideal machine would do.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Mach-Zehnder Lab?
chunks.text: One photon enters from the source, meets a beam splitter, takes two arms, and meets a second beam splitter before reaching the top or bottom detector. The phase slider (or the 0, 90, 180 and 270 degree buttons) turns the phase of the bottom arm. The arm blocker puts an obstacle in the top or bottom arm. Fire 1 or Fire 100 sends photons and the bars show where they landed, against the dashed prediction. The curve shows the odds at every phase, and the bonus bomb test uses a hidden object.

chunks.heading: What does the phase do to the two detectors?
chunks.text: With nothing blocked, the chance of the top detector is sin squared of phi over two and the bottom is cos squared of phi over two. At 0 degrees the paths cancel at the top and add at the bottom, so only the bottom clicks. At 180 degrees it flips. In between, the chance moves smoothly, with 50% each at 90 degrees. This pattern is interference.

chunks.heading: Does the photon really split in two?
chunks.text: No. A photon is always found whole, at one detector. What takes both arms is its probability amplitude, and the two routes add up like waves at the second beam splitter. Where they add the photon is likely to land, and where they cancel it never does. Fire many photons and the pattern appears even though each one lands in a single place.

chunks.heading: Why does blocking an arm make the interference vanish?
chunks.text: With one arm blocked there is only one route left to the second splitter, so there is nothing to interfere with. The photon is then sent 50/50 to each detector, with half of all photons absorbed by the blocker. That gives 25% at each detector, at every phase. Knowing which path the photon took removes the interference.

chunks.heading: How does the bomb test work?
chunks.text: The phase is fixed at 0 degrees, so with an empty arm the top detector never clicks. If an object sits in the bottom arm, the interference is destroyed and the top detector can click. A click at the top proves an object is there, and the photon was not absorbed. With an object present, 50% of the time the photon is absorbed (a bang), 25% the top detector clicks (found safely) and 25% the bright detector clicks (no information).

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Mach-Zehnder Lab?
chunks.text: Probabilities are not the whole story: the two routes add as amplitudes, so they can cancel, which is what makes one detector go dark. Block a route, or learn which path the photon took, and the cancellation disappears. The model is idealised: perfect 50/50 splitters, no losses, one photon at a time.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Two-Qubit Lab?
chunks.text: Alice and Bob each hold one qubit and both start at 0. Apply H, X, Z, S or T to either one, or a CNOT in either direction. Measure collapses a qubit and Reset to 00 starts again. The meter shows how entangled the pair is (concurrence, from 0 to 1). Each qubit's own panel shows whether it still has a state of its own. Measure the pair 20 times shows 20 results. The goal is a Bell pair: H on Alice, then CNOT with Alice as control.

chunks.heading: What does the entanglement meter show?
chunks.text: It is the concurrence of the pair's pure state: 0 when the two qubits each have their own state, and 1 for a maximally entangled pair such as a Bell pair. In between, the qubits are partly entangled. It is twice the size of (a00 times a11, minus a01 times a10), where each a is the amplitude of that result.

chunks.heading: Why does each qubit alone show no state when the pair is entangled?
chunks.text: In an entangled pair the information is in the relationship between the qubits, not in either one. Looked at on its own, each qubit is a perfectly random coin, which is a Bloch arrow of length zero. The pair as a whole does have a definite state. That is why the panels say no state for each qubit, while the pair's bars show a clear pattern.

chunks.heading: Why do the two qubits always agree in a Bell pair?
chunks.text: A Bell pair is an equal mix of 00 and 11 and nothing else. So whichever answer one qubit gives, the other gives the same, but which answer comes up is random. The 20 measurements show it: every pair reads 00 or 11, about half of each, and no pair ever disagrees.

chunks.heading: Why does measuring one qubit change the meter?
chunks.text: Measuring collapses the pair into one definite result, so afterwards each qubit has its own state again and the entanglement is gone. To explore again, press Reset to 00. This is why the meter drops to zero after a measurement.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Two-Qubit Lab?
chunks.text: Entanglement is a property of the pair: the pair can have a perfectly definite state while neither qubit has one. Correlated answers on their own are not strange, because two matching coins would do that, so the point is that no script prepared in advance can imitate the correlations (see the Bell and CHSH Explorer). The meter works for a pure two-qubit state only.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Bell and CHSH Explorer?
chunks.text: Alice and Bob share an entangled pair, and each picks a measurement angle depending on a question. The four sliders set Alice's angle for question 0 and 1 and Bob's angle for question 0 and 1. The value S combines the four correlations. Use the best angles sets them to the strongest setting. Play 100 rounds or 1000 rounds plays the CHSH game with your angles, and the table shows each correlation.

chunks.heading: What does the value S mean?
chunks.text: S is the sum of three correlations minus one, each running from +1 (always agree) to -1 (always differ). Any shared pre-agreed script, a local hidden variable, can reach at most 2 in size. Quantum mechanics reaches up to 2 times the square root of 2, about 2.83. Seeing the size of S above 2 is the Bell violation.

chunks.heading: Why can a shared plan not go above 2?
chunks.text: With a plan, every answer is fixed in advance, so each of the four correlations is either +1 or -1 for that plan. Three of them can be +1, but then the fourth is forced to agree too, and since it is subtracted the sum is at most 2 in size. Averages of plans cannot do better. The entangled pair does not follow a fixed plan, which is how it gets past 2.

chunks.heading: Does passing 2 let Alice and Bob send messages?
chunks.text: No. Each person's own results look completely random whatever the other does. The correlation only shows up when the two lists of results are put side by side, which needs an ordinary message. So Bell tests rule out local hidden variables, and do not give a way to signal faster than light.

chunks.heading: Which angles give the largest S?
chunks.text: Alice's two angles should be 45 degrees apart, with Bob's two angles sitting halfway between them, one on each side. For example, Alice at 0 and 45 degrees and Bob at 22.5 and -22.5 degrees gives S equal to 2 times the square root of 2 and a CHSH win rate of about 85.4%. The Use the best angles button sets these.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Bell and CHSH Explorer?
chunks.text: The correlation between the two measurements follows a smooth wave in the angle gap, and a shared script can only trace a zig-zag with the same corner points. That difference is what the Bell test detects. The lab is exact for an ideal Bell pair, with no noise, so in a real experiment the value of S is a little lower.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Teleportation Lab?
chunks.text: Choose the message Alice wants to send, either with the named buttons or the tilt and turn sliders. Then step through the protocol with the button: make the Bell pair, entangle the message with Alice's half, apply a Hadamard, measure, and correct. The two spheres show the message and Bob's qubit, and the bar shows how well Bob's qubit matches. After the measurement you can untick Alice's two bits reach Bob. Teleport 200 times repeats the whole thing.

chunks.heading: Why does Bob not have the message before he gets the bits?
chunks.text: After Alice measures, Bob's qubit holds the message but scrambled by one of four possible flips, and which one depends on Alice's random result. Without her two bits Bob cannot tell which, so averaged over her outcomes his qubit is pure noise. Untick Alice's bits reach Bob to see that: he is wrong unless the bits happened to be 00.

chunks.heading: Why does teleportation not beat the speed of light?
chunks.text: The bits have to travel by an ordinary route, so the message cannot arrive before they do. Before the bits arrive, Bob's qubit is useless as a message. The entanglement was prepared earlier and only makes the transfer possible, which is why nothing is sent faster than light.

chunks.heading: Where does the original qubit go?
chunks.text: Alice's measurement destroys it: her message qubit becomes a plain 0 or 1 that tells her nothing about the message. The state has been moved to Bob, not copied. Copying an unknown quantum state is impossible, which is the no-cloning theorem. Only the state travels, not matter or energy.

chunks.heading: What does the match percentage mean?
chunks.text: It is how close Bob's qubit is to the message: 100% is an exact match, and 50% is what a random guess would score. Each step moves it, and after the correction it should read 100% for any message. A short arrow on Bob's sphere means his qubit is still tangled up with Alice's.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Teleportation Lab?
chunks.text: A quantum state can be moved with one shared entangled pair and two ordinary bits, and it works for any message you choose. Each of the four bit pairs comes up about a quarter of the time, whatever the message is. The simulation follows the real textbook protocol exactly on three qubits.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Deutsch-Jozsa Explorer?
chunks.text: Choose how many input bits the function has. Pick a preset function or tap cells of the truth table to flip f(x) for each input. The signs show what the function does to each input after one query. Run the circuit once reads the input qubits, and the verdict reads: all zeros means constant, anything else means balanced. The Queries to be sure panel compares how many questions a classical and a quantum detective need.

chunks.heading: What is a constant and a balanced function?
chunks.text: The function takes an n-bit input and returns 0 or 1. It is constant if it gives the same answer for every input, and balanced if it gives 0 for exactly half the inputs and 1 for the other half. The algorithm promises to work only when the function is one of these two. If you flip cells so it is neither, the lab warns that the promise is broken.

chunks.heading: Why does reading all zeros mean constant?
chunks.text: After the oracle, each input has a plus or minus sign depending on f. The final Hadamards make those signs interfere. When all signs are the same, they add up on the all-zeros outcome and the readout is always all zeros. When half are plus and half minus, they cancel exactly on all zeros, so it never appears. So one run is enough to tell them apart for certain.

chunks.heading: Why are there signs after the oracle?
chunks.text: The extra helper qubit is prepared so that asking the function flips its sign instead of a bit. This is called phase kickback. Every input then carries a sign of plus one or minus one, according to f(x), and all inputs are asked at the same time because they are in superposition.

chunks.heading: How many queries does a classical computer need?
chunks.text: To be certain, a classical detective may have to look at more than half of the inputs, which is half of them plus one, in the worst case. The quantum circuit needs one. The gap grows exponentially in n, but it is a speed-up only against a classical algorithm that must be certain, and this problem has no practical use.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Deutsch-Jozsa Explorer?
chunks.text: Interference can settle a question with one query that a classical method has to check many times. The oracle here is given as a truth table, so the lab shows the idea and not a real-world speed-up. Real speed-ups need an oracle that is cheap to build as a circuit.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Grover Explorer?
chunks.text: Choose the size of the list (4, 8 or 16 items). Tap an item to hide the prize under it; you can mark up to half the list. Each tap of Grover round applies one round of the algorithm. The bars show the amplitude of every item, positive up and negative down, and the dashed line is their average. The number and the bar show the chance that a measurement finds a marked item. The back button returns to the start.

chunks.heading: What does one Grover round do?
chunks.text: A round has two steps. First the oracle flips the sign of the marked amplitude. Then every amplitude is reflected about the average, so each becomes twice the average minus itself. The marked one, now below the average, ends up higher than before, and all the others sink a little. Repeating the round raises the marked amplitude step by step.

chunks.heading: Why do too many rounds make the chance fall again?
chunks.text: Grover's rounds are a rotation of the state, so after the best round the state keeps turning and carries the answer away again. The chance of success follows sin squared of (2k plus 1) times theta, which rises, peaks and falls. The lab shows the best number of rounds, and stopping there is part of the algorithm.

chunks.heading: How much faster is Grover than a classical search?
chunks.text: About the square root of N. A classical search of an unsorted list needs around N over 2 guesses on average, while Grover needs about pi over 4 times the square root of N rounds. That is a quadratic speed-up, not an exponential one. For a handful of items the classical search is just as good, and the gap only matters for huge lists.

chunks.heading: What changes if I mark more than one item?
chunks.text: Each round turns the state by the same angle, but the angle is larger when more items are marked, so you need fewer rounds. The best number of rounds is about pi over 4 times the square root of N over M, for M marked items out of N. With half the list marked a random guess is already right half the time, so there is little for the algorithm to gain.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Grover Explorer?
chunks.text: Amplitude is moved onto the answer by interference: a sign flip and a reflection about the average. The algorithm is a rotation, so it can overshoot. It gives a square-root speed-up and needs a way to check an answer inside the quantum circuit. The lab is an exact simulation.

chunks.heading: How do I use the Noise Lab?
chunks.text: Choose how many qubits hold one qubit's worth of information (1 is no protection). The slider sets the chance that each qubit flips. Run trials repeats the noise many times and compares one bare qubit with the group. The bars show how often the information is lost, against the maths prediction, and the curve shows the failure rate at every noise level. The section Find the error without looking at the data compares qubits with a helper and fixes a flip.

chunks.heading: Why is the code better than a single qubit?
chunks.text: The group takes a vote: the information is lost only if more than half of the qubits flip. For three qubits that needs two or three flips, which is much rarer than one flip when the noise is small. The chance falls from p to 3p squared minus 2p cubed. With 5 or more qubits it falls further, as long as the noise is below 50%.

chunks.heading: Why does the code get worse when the noise is above 50%?
chunks.text: A qubit that flips more often than not is more likely to be wrong than right, so a vote among such qubits is more likely to come out wrong too. At exactly 50% the code and a single qubit are equally bad. Real codes have a much lower break-even point, around 1% per operation, which is why today's qubits are not yet good enough for useful error correction.

chunks.heading: How can the helper find the error without reading the data?
chunks.text: The helper qubit only compares two data qubits and says whether they agree or differ. It never learns what either one holds, so the encoded superposition is untouched. Two comparisons, Q1 with Q2 and Q2 with Q3, point at a single flipped qubit. The panel shows that the amplitudes of the data are the same before and after the probes.

chunks.heading: Why do two flips fool the code?
chunks.text: The code assumes the odd qubit out is the one that flipped. When two qubits flip, the odd one out is actually the healthy one, so the repair flips the wrong qubit and the whole encoded qubit ends up flipped. The code can undo one flip at a time. That is the reason its failure rate is not zero.

chunks.heading: What should I notice in the Noise Lab?
chunks.text: Errors can be found without reading the data, and a group of noisy qubits can be more reliable than one, as long as the noise is rare enough. This is a simplified model: only bit flips, every qubit flips independently, and the probes and gates are perfect. Real machines also have phase flips and errors in the checks themselves, so real codes are bigger.
